item.title: Six Flags shuts down X2 rollercoaster after more than 100 allege brain injuries
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw14d37446d8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Six Flags shuts down X2 rollercoaster after more than 100 allege brain injuries - Published Six Flags Magic Mountain, an amusement park in California, has announced it will permanently close a popular rollercoaster after more than 100 riders alleged they suffered brain injuries. The X2 rollercoaster, one of the park's main attractions, with long wait times to ride and seats that spin 360 degrees, has been closed since July. Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do". The decision comes after lawsuits and news reports alleged that riders suffered brain injuries after riding X2. A law firm representing some of the plaintiffs said the decision had come "too late" for its clients. Announcing the closure on Tuesday, , external Six Flags Magic Mountain Park President Brian Oerding said: "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously." Dordick Law Corporation, who filed civil lawsuits against the park, said it had been contacted by about 400 people who alleged they had injuries they believed were caused by the ride. "They got on X2 expecting a thrill. Instead, they left with catastrophic brain injuries," the firm said in a statement. "Some needed emergency brain surgery. Some are still fighting to get their lives back." The law firm said that while it welcomed the closure of the ride to protect future guests, "it does nothing for the people who have already been hurt". Originally called X, the ride first opened in 2002 but was closed months later for repairs to design flaws, the Los Angeles Times reports. It was then closed again in 2007 to replace its trains with lighter versions. It reopened the following year as X2 and since then has been ridden by more than 16 million people, the park said. A law firm that represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding X2 in 2022, said the closure was not enough. While the Hawley family is "relieved to hear that Six Flags is finally closing the X2, it does not change the fact that Christopher Hawley was killed by a dangerous roller coaster that was allowed to operate for nearly two decades," attorney Brent Wisner of Wisner Baum LLP said in a statement to the BBC. Hawley's family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August. "That tragedy cannot be undone," Wisner said, calling for legal reform, proactive regulation and proper governmental oversight. "We cannot rely on profit-centered corporations to do the right thing only after enough people have been hurt," he added. "We hope that whatever replaces the X2 is safe."

item.title: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck8d3vl9mj13o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner - Published A brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing". Backpack's wideness narrowly defeated a bear known only as 910, earning 103,344 votes to 910's 98,253 in the final round of the competition, which is run by the Katmai National Park in Alaska. The National Parks Service thanked the 16 bears who "involuntarily participated" in the competition, now in its thirteenth year. Backpack, who was described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months. His mother Holly was the 2019 Fat Bear Week winner. Backpack's name derives not from what another supporter described as the "light bulb shape" of his body, but his habit, as a cub, of climbing onto Holly's back when she waded through the park's salmon-filled Brooks River. Another supporter described him as being a "big fuzzy boy". But Backpack was not without his detractors. One person said she felt that Bear 910, a female who raised both her biological cub and an adopted niece, was a "larger bear all around. Backpack just has a bigger booty". "I just feel like 910 really put in the work this year," another 910 fan wrote on the park's Facebook page, while a voter commented, "She round, she thick my girl 910 got my vote." The finalists' latest weights have not yet been revealed. But adult male brown bears average up to 408kg in mid-summer and often pack on the equivalent of 25% of their body weight by autumn. The largest males can weigh more than 540kg. Females are smaller but can reach weights of over 300kg. Cubs are born weighing roughly half a kilogram. "During hibernation, bears do not eat or drink and lose one-third of their body weight. Their winter survival depends on accumulating ample fat reserves before entering the den," organisers wrote. From June until mid October, the bears gorge on food, including salmon caught with their jaws or paws. Backpack's biography says his "quiet toughness has allowed him to find his niche alongside the biggest bears at Brooks River". Last year, over 1.7 million votes were cast from more than 100 countries to crown the competition's heavyweight champion. Related topics - Published17 September

item.title: South Korea demands apology from Pyongyang for landmine blasts that injured three
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwj3dkvpm4e7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
South Korea demands apology from Pyongyang for landmine blasts that injured three - Published South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month. Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September. South Korea said on Tuesday it was "certain" that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, came from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what he said was a violation of a decades-old armistice. North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation". Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea. Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making." South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border. South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War. That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5-mile) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas. In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ. In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied. Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now. Ties between Pyongyang and Seoul have only deteriorated since 2015, raising the risk of friction when such incidents happen. Christopher Green, a senior consultant with Crisis Group, tells the BBC that "The North Koreans have been wilfully attempting to harden the border [and] eliminate inter-Korean relations". As a result, he adds, the two Koreas no longer have the "same low-level communication" that they shared in 2015. "Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he says. The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms". "UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said.

item.title: Dozens hurt and hundreds arrested in wave of French school protests
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c862epne7glyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Dozens hurt and hundreds arrested in wave of French school protests - Published Four-hundred-and-forty people, mostly minors, have been arrested and 76 injured as a wave of school protests over overcrowded classes and teacher shortages spreads across France, officials say. The demonstrations began in Paris last week but have escalated to cities including Dijon, Lyon, Strasbourg, Lille and Marseille, with teenagers blockading their schools for days. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said while some of the students' demands were legitimate what worried him was the violence. He spoke of one young man having lost the use of part of his hand after firing a mortar firework. The dozens hurt since the start of protests included both pupils and staff, he said. Secondary school students' union USL says as many as 400 of France's 3,700 lycées for 15-18 year-olds have been blockaded and it has called for further action on Thursday, including at universities. Firefighters were called out in Strasbourg after bins were set alight outside a school, while in Dijon police used tear gas to disperse dozens of students, French media reported on Wednesday. On Tuesday alone, at least 10 teachers and several students were hurt, according to the education minister, who added that one teacher had been beaten up. Geffray singled out the radical left party La France Insoumise (LFI - France Unbowed) for stirring up trouble. The LFI mayor of northern Paris suburb Seine-Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, who has praised the protesters, has been criticised for suggesting that in some cases "violence can be legitimate" when a teenager is faced with riot police firing so-called "flashballs". "Every time we try to express ourselves we get tear-gassed, they don't try to understand us," students at the Paul-Éluard lycée in Saint-Denis told France Inter radio. "When we try to talk about our rights, they tear-gas us, they hit us." For days students have blockaded the lycée in Saint-Denis, and part of the school gate has been torn down. Bagayoko was pictured on Monday dancing with protesting students outside the school and singing the Marseillaise with them, prompting Valérie Pécresse, the conservative head of the Île-de-France region that includes Paris, to demand he pays for some of the damage. Reports from several cities have spoken of protesters hurling projectiles at police, who then responded with tear gas and sometimes batons. One student suffered a serious eye injury near a school in Tours on Wednesday, amid unconfirmed reports he had been hit by a flashball fired by police. There were further arrests on Wednesday in Nancy in the east and the Gironde region in the south-west. A teacher was left in shock on Tuesday in the northern city of Lille, where he was reportedly attacked after trying to ring the fire brigade to report a burning bin. One 16-year-old female student said they were trying to deliver a message. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason," she told AFP news agency. "We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked." Ryad Rani, president of the USL, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force. When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has come in for criticism from some politicians, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner". The movement began last week in the Île-de-France region. As it began to spread, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned that any escalation would be "irresponsible". Students' union USL has now called for a large national protest on 6 October. Tuesday's protests coincided with nationwide walkouts by unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions. Nuñez said the broader public sector protests, with at least 200,000 participants reported, mostly went without incident. - Published2 days ago

item.title: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9kgvm275ev8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea - Published A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say. Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer. The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent". The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported. The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said. "People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent." In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues. The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400). Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery. Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province. Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition. Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.

item.title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2z92xx57no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing - Published Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die. Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped. The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes. "Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media. He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door. When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane". "I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said. "We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure." Hayun said he then jumped back into the cockpit and "started pulling the controls". When asked by Netanyahu whether he knew what he was doing, the passenger answered: "I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister." Hayun said the plane then started to level out. By then, two on-duty pilots who had been in the passenger cabin were at the front of the plane, and one told Hayun he was taking control from there. Netanyahu praised Hayun, calling him a "great hero" and a "lion". Another passenger, Zvika Meness, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan he helped overpower the attacker, and the passenger and two others "tied him up with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones". "Another pilot who was sitting in the passenger cabin went in to replace the additional pilot, and they essentially landed the plane," he added. The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft. They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags. "Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control". Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment". "Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added. A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane". The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery". The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given. US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack. - Published12 minutes ago - Published19 minutes ago

item.title: Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme30dz5vkzko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit - Published US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age". The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry. The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity. Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House. 1. AI 'self-regulation' pact Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting. The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues. They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways." The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. "It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president." Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board. Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation". Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins". But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord. Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents. It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney. The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said. "The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added. - Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings - Published16 September - Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? - Published17 September Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight over the technology. On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns. The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation. Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards". The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added. 2. Doubling down on data centres Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI. The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the US over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on communities. Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November. A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas. Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters. The president previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor". Huang, whose company produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories". These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added. 3. It's now 'Super Intelligence' Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence. SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said. "As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said. During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake". Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term. With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said. But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems. - Published1 day ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9qr8jy8ynyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail - Published US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy. In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him. "I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game". Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal. Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false. On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story. They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place". The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service. "It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned." What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd. Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state. "I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years." That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap. "I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right. Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home. The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov, an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany. "They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically." Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace. He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space. "That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine." Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright. "I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to." But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently." Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed. Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long". When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again." Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions. He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped. And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend. "I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better." item.title: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjkg7k6z9296o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign - Published Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city. "Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says. Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September. "All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains. Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded. "We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC. At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again. Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times. This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia. Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another. Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko. Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action. "Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far." The damage to the metals industry could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's economy and society. Ukraine had 12 metallurgical plants before losing parts of its industrial heartland in the east shortly after the start of hostilities with Russia in 2014. By 2018, there were just nine, and three years into the full-scale war in 2025 that number had fallen to six. Among those lost were the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, Ukraine's south-eastern city captured after a months-long Russian siege. Among the steel-making cities caught up in Russia's recent missile campaign is President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city of Kryvyi Rih. On 25 September, Ukraine's biggest steelworks, Arcelor Mittal Kryvyi Rih, announced it was unable to reopen after repeated attacks over five weeks, praising the bravery of its workers, five of whom had died. Latest on war in Ukraine - Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished? - Published20 September Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs. The situation, he admitted, was very difficult. "It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things." Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center. "In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC. "This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average." If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming." The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction. Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia. Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware. "We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv. There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added. Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon. Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery. "Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't." EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine. But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat. His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed. "This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

item.title: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg8dxrv54do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels - Published One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence. Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation. Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack. But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad. Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus. Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised. By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed. University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home. Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate. What happened? The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier. The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed. BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered. Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge. Behind the gates, students described a night of fear. "We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here." Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here." So why have police lodged a case? That the police open a case and investigate the allegation was among the protesters' central demands. "The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC. Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred. Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room. "As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said. But they are continuing to examine the footage. "The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this." Why did the protests grow so large? It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself. There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university. "We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield." Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played. Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own. On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them. The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations. Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases. What is happening now? For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians. Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest. The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety. The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed? Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest. "I feel students can't do this," she said. Watch: Luxury prison in Indonesia demolished after public outcry A prison compound in Indonesia has been demolished after public outcry following the discovery of luxury apartments on its grounds. Investigators reported finding luxury facilities in Cibinong Prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, allegedly used by favoured inmates during a surprise inspection on 23 September. The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex. Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff. The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia's prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery. Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal amid floods Massive flooding left a government building in western Nepal teetering on the edge of an unstable ledge before it fell into the Daram River. Witnesses captured the moment that the building in Baglung collapsed on Sunday, 27 September. Officials removed important documents and computers from the building before it fell, local ward chair Tej Thapa confirmed to the BBC. No one was injured. Landslides and floods have killed at least 27 people over recent days, according to Nepal's national disaster agency, only weeks after a flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border killed 1,400 people and left thousands more missing. Fires and blockades as students stage school protests across France More than 400 people, most of them children, were arrested in France on Tuesday during a wave of school protests across the country. The country's interior minister Laurent Nuñez told broadcaster BFMTV that 440 people in total had been detained, while 48 law enforcement members had been injured. Students are demonstrating over issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. France's education ministry said 400 schools were impacted by protests or disruptions on Tuesday. The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris. The protests on Tuesday came the same day as professionals from public sectors - including teachers and firefighters - also demonstrated against planned budget cuts in France. Close-up look at Turner's '£50m' Rome painting on show in the city A renowned painting by British landscape artist JMW Turner has returned to the city that inspired it nearly two centuries ago. Rome, from Mount Aventine features a panoramic view of the Italian capital and will be on display at the Palazzo Rondinini for three days. Dating back to the 19th century, the masterpiece was based on sketches made in Rome. The work of art is remarkably well preserved and is believed to have never been restored. It even features traces of fingerprints and brush hairs are still visible. The painting has only been to auction once before, selling for more than £30 million. Sotheby's now expects it could fetch around £50 million when it goes under the hammer in London this December. The BBC's Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Sarah Rainsford, had a close-up look at the painting in Rome.
